newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai Airways aims to regain lost premier status.
newsitem.headline: Thai Airways aims to regain lost premier status.

text.p: Thai Airways International Plc is counting on a five-year expansion plan to help it regain its lost premier status, industry analysts said on Friday.
The former high-flier dropped out of the list of top-10 airlines in the world in 1994.
The analysts said Thai faced an uphill battle against rivals Singapore Airlines and Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd while it operated under a government austerity policy hampering its growth.
The airline is 93 percent owned by the Thai government.
Thai on Thursday appeared as if it was bowing to government pressure to help the country trim foreign exchange spending and narrow its current account deficit.

Chairman Mahidol Chantrangkul said the airline would hold talks with the finance ministry on a state guideline for it to lease, rather than buy, 21 new aircraft worth 68.8 billion baht ($2.75 billion) between now and 2000.
Thai Airways had earlier planned to finance the acquisition by borrowing 40 percent in the domestic money market with the rest being met by foreign financing.
He said the company's board had already agreed to lease four Boeing 777-200s and two 747-400s worth 22.98 billion baht that it planned to take delivery of this year.
Analysts said leasing aircraft would raise their financing costs at a time that the carrier aimed to improve efficiency by cutting operating expenses.
"It is critical to improve performance by cutting (operating) cost, by modernising its fleet," said Virachart Kasempibunchai of Securities One Plc.

The carrier's five-year plan calls for reduction in the 14 models of aircraft and 11 models of engine in its current fleet to six each by 2000. Fewer aircraft and engine models save maintenance and pilot training costs.
Analysts said Singapore Airlines and Cathay currently operated only three to four aircraft models.
"The Thai Airways fleet is currently about the same size as that of Singapore Airlines or Cathay, but Singapore will definitely surge far ahead soon," Virachart said.
The Thai plan calls for 8.5 percent annual growth in passengers. The airline flew 14.3 million passengers in the year ending September 30, 1996.
Thai will retire 31 planes by the end of 2000. After the new acquisitions the fleet will grow to 78 from 73 now.
Analysts said Thai must shake off its long-standing image as a state enterprise weakened by political and military meddling in its management. ($1 = 25 baht)
